summary: A landlocked country on the southern edge of the Sahara in West Africa, once the core of the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire; Timbuktu was a major center of Islamic learning in the Middle Ages.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the Middle Ages with the Saharan caravans; the rulers and merchants of the Mali and Songhai empires were the first to accept it, and Timbuktu became a center of learning. The jihads launched by the Fulani in the 18th–19th centuries (such as El Hadj Umar Tall's Toucouleur Empire) spread Islam in the countryside, and during the colonial period Sufi orders penetrated further everywhere. Today Muslims are the great majority, but many still blend in traditional customs.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced during the French colonial period of 1892–1960 by the Catholic White Fathers and others, spreading mainly among the Dogon and Bobo in the south and in the cities. Protestantism was brought by American missionary groups in the 20th century. Christians are a minority in Mali, but the churches run schools and medical institutions.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Mali's ethnic groups have rich traditional beliefs, such as the Dogon cosmology and mask rituals and the Komo and other secret societies of the Bambara. Those who follow only traditional religion are mainly in rural areas of the south and center, and many Muslims and Christians also still take part in these rituals.

religion.background: Islam arrived in West Africa in the 8th–11th centuries with the Berber and Arab caravans crossing the Sahara, and the merchant class of the Ghana Empire was the first to accept it. The rulers of the Mali Empire and Songhai Empire of the 13th–16th centuries were Muslims; in 1324 the Malian king Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge entourage and astonished Cairo with his large amounts of gold, while Timbuktu and Djenné became centers of Islamic learning. But it was not until the Fulani jihad movements of the 18th–19th centuries and the colonial period that Islam spread on a large scale in the countryside. Catholicism arrived during the French colonial period of 1892–1960. In 2012 the north was occupied by Islamist extremist organizations, and the saints' tombs of Timbuktu were destroyed.

language.official: The 2023 constitution makes 13 indigenous languages official languages, and French a working language.

ranking.name: Bambara
ranking.description: Bambara belongs to the Mande group and is a close relative of the Malinke of the 13th-century Mali Empire; after the Bambara founded the Ségou Kingdom in the 18th century their influence grew. Today it is the main language of the capital Bamako and the south, and the most common lingua franca of markets and broadcasting across the country, spoken by about 80 percent of the population. The 2023 constitution made it one of the official languages.

ranking.name: Fula
ranking.description: Fula is the language of the Fulani (Peul), a nomadic West African people who live by herding cattle and are spread across the whole Sahel. In the 19th century the Fulani founded the Massina Empire in central Mali, and Fula is most common in the Mopti region of the Inner Niger Delta.

ranking.name: Songhai
ranking.description: Songhai was the language of the Songhai Empire of the 15th–16th centuries, which had Gao as its capital and controlled trade on the middle Niger. After Moroccan forces broke the Songhai Empire in 1591, Songhai continued in northern cities along the Niger such as Gao and Timbuktu, and it is still the main language there.

language.history: Mali has dozens of languages, belonging mainly to the Niger–Congo family (the Mande group's Bambara, the Fula, etc.) and the Nilo-Saharan family (Songhai), with Tamasheq of the Berber group (the Tuareg) also in the north. In the Mali Empire period Mande was the court language, and the oral tradition was passed down in song by griots (hereditary storytellers), the Epic of Sundiata being a representative example. During French colonial rule of 1892–1960, French became the language of administration and education. The 2023 constitution removed French's status as an official language, making it a "working language", and recognized 13 indigenous languages as official languages.

ranking.name: Tigadèguèna (peanut stew)
ranking.description: Meat (beef, lamb or chicken) and vegetables stewed in peanut butter, with a thick, sweet sauce, eaten with white rice. It has a rich, sweet flavor and is a common home-style dish across West Africa.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and were brought to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, quickly becoming an important crop there. During the colonial period France promoted peanuts vigorously in Senegambia and Mali as an export cash crop, and peanuts thus entered the daily diet. Tigadèguèna means "peanut butter" in Bambara; it shares its origin with Senegal's mafé and is thought to be associated with the Malinke, and today it is Mali's most popular home-style dish.

ranking.name: Tô (millet porridge)
ranking.description: A thick porridge ball cooked from millet or sorghum flour and water, eaten with a sauce stewed from okra or baobab leaves. It has a dense texture and is mainly eaten to accompany various sauces.
ranking.history: Tô is the most basic staple of Mali and the Sahel; millet and sorghum have been grown in West Africa for thousands of years and are drought- and heat-tolerant, suited to the dry climate of the Sahel. Traditionally women pound the grain with a wooden mortar and then cook it outdoors in a large pot, and the rhythm of pounding is an everyday scene in Malian villages. The whole family gathers around a large dish and pinches off tô with the right hand, the typical way of eating in a Malian household.

ranking.name: Riz au gras (tomato meat rice)
ranking.description: A red, oily rice made by stewing tomato, onion and meat and then cooking the rice together in the sauce. The grains absorb the rich flavor of the tomato and meat juices and taste fragrant and rich.
ranking.history: Riz au gras means "fatty rice" and shares its origin with West Africa's jollof rice, which is generally thought to originate with the Wolof Empire in the Senegambia region around the 14th century. The Inner Niger Delta has grown African rice since ancient times, and Mali has a long rice culture. In Mali this dish is the feast dish for weddings, baptisms and festivals such as Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

ranking.name: Dégué (millet yogurt dessert)
ranking.description: A dessert or drink made by mixing steamed millet grains with fermented milk or yogurt and sugar. It has a creamy, sweet and tangy texture and is best served cold.
ranking.history: Dégué comes from the food of the Fulani, a nomadic people of the Sahel who live by herding cattle, whose main food is fermented milk; combined with locally grown millet, it forms this dessert. In hot Mali, chilled dégué is a refreshing treat, and it is also often drunk at the breaking of the fast during Ramadan. Today it is popular in many countries of West Africa.

ranking.name: Fonio
ranking.description: An ancient African grain with extremely tiny grains, which can be steamed and eaten like couscous or cooked into porridge. It has a light texture with a faint nutty aroma.
ranking.history: Fonio is one of the oldest cultivated grains of West Africa and has been grown in the Sahel for thousands of years. It has a short growing season, tolerates drought, and can grow on poor soil; it was once regarded as "food for the poor" and also has an important place in Dogon myth. Because it is hard to hull, fonio declined for a time, but in recent years it has gained attention in international markets for being gluten-free and highly nutritious.
